logline: Fictional Vice President Selina Meyer and her catastrophically incompetent team discover that political power is mostly just the management of humiliation.

renewal.note: Seven seasons concluded on May 12, 2019. Julia Louis-Dreyfus won six consecutive Emmy Awards for Outstanding Lead Actress in a Comedy Series for the role.

bollymeter.basis: Season 1 earned 78% on Rotten Tomatoes and a Metacritic 72. The Hank Stuever at The Washington Post called it 'instantly engaging and outrageously fun.' The show was still calibrating its satirical targets but the lead performance was already exceptional.

pull_quotes.text: Thanks to Louis-Dreyfus, and the show's remarkable knack for dialogue and timing, Veep is instantly engaging and outrageously fun.

seasons.review_body: Veep's first season arrived in April 2012 trailing the considerable pedigree of creator Armando Iannucci's BBC series The Thick of It. The 78% Rotten Tomatoes score and Metacritic 72 reflected genuine enthusiasm for Julia Louis-Dreyfus's lead performance and the show's surgical dialogue, alongside hesitation about whether the political satire had the edge of its British predecessor. Hank Stuever at The Washington Post called it 'instantly engaging and outrageously fun.' The ensemble - Anna Chlumsky, Tony Hale, Reid Scott - quickly emerged as one of television's finest comedic combinations.

bollymeter.basis: Season 3 achieved a perfect 100% on Rotten Tomatoes and Metacritic 86. Brandon Nowalk at The A.V. Club wrote it had 'become the clearest heir to 30 Rock and Arrested Development.' David Hiltbrand at The Philadelphia Inquirer called it 'the sharpest Beltway satire the medium has ever seen.'

pull_quotes.text: Veep has become the clearest heir to 30 Rock and Arrested Development.

seasons.review_body: Season 3 was the season where Veep graduated from promising satire to essential television. The perfect 100% Rotten Tomatoes score and Metacritic 86 reflected a press consensus that the series had found its singular voice: a comedy of political catastrophe where everyone is too self-interested to recognise their own incompetence. Brandon Nowalk at The A.V. Club wrote it had 'become the clearest heir to 30 Rock and Arrested Development.' David Hiltbrand at The Philadelphia Inquirer called it 'the sharpest Beltway satire the medium has ever seen.' Louis-Dreyfus's Selina Meyer was now one of television's great comic creations.
seasons.season_over_season: The leap from Season 2 to Season 3 is the show finding its ceiling - the satire sharpens, the ensemble is perfectly deployed, and the political nihilism becomes the joke rather than merely the backdrop.

bollymeter.basis: Season 4 scored a second consecutive 100% on Rotten Tomatoes and Metacritic 90. Tim Goodman at The Hollywood Reporter declared it 'the most thoroughly assured, hilarious and brilliantly written and acted' run of episodes in the series.

pull_quotes.text: Veep delivers its most thoroughly assured, hilarious and brilliantly written and acted episodes.

seasons.review_body: Season 4 is the series at its technical and satirical peak. The 100% Rotten Tomatoes score and Metacritic 90 - the highest the show would ever reach - reflected that Iannucci had created something genuinely irreplaceable. Tim Goodman at The Hollywood Reporter wrote that the season entered 'firmly established as one of television's best comedies, and then immediately does what seems impossible - it delivers its most thoroughly assured, hilarious and brilliantly written and acted episodes.' The season's escalating crises around Selina's presidential run gave the ensemble's collective incompetence a dramatic urgency the earlier seasons had not needed.
seasons.season_over_season: Season 4 is the series at its technical and satirical peak - the 100% Rotten Tomatoes score was matched only by Season 3, but the dramatic stakes here land harder.

episode_reviews.title: Election Night
episode_reviews.spoiler_free: The Season 4 finale stages Selina's election night across one sustained comedic pressure-cooker, extracting maximum farce from the gap between political ambition and reality. The vote count sequence is a masterclass in sustained comic timing across an ensemble of seven people all talking past each other.
episode_reviews.the_moment: The vote count sequence - seven people in one room, all talking past each other, and every line landing.

critic_note.text: Veep delivers its most thoroughly assured, hilarious and brilliantly written and acted episodes.

bollymeter.basis: The final season scored 97% on Rotten Tomatoes and Metacritic 87. David Hiltbrand at The Philadelphia Inquirer had called Veep 'the sharpest Beltway satire the medium has ever seen' - the finale did not disprove that claim.

pull_quotes.text: HBO's Veep is the sharpest Beltway satire the medium has ever seen.

seasons.review_body: Season 7 brought Veep to a close with 97% on Rotten Tomatoes and Metacritic 87. The press response to the finale debated the specific resolution while broadly agreeing it was earned and thematically consistent: the show's argument - that political ambition is indistinguishable from pathology - demanded a conclusion without redemption, and the writers delivered one. Julia Louis-Dreyfus, who won six consecutive Emmy Awards for the role, received extensive praise at the Hollywood Foreign Press for her work in the final stretch. The seven-episode run felt economical rather than truncated. David Hiltbrand's earlier Philadelphia Inquirer assessment that Veep was 'the sharpest Beltway satire the medium has ever seen' held through the finale.
seasons.season_over_season: A shorter final run than peak seasons but no creative compromise - the show ends as it lived, with Selina Meyer the funniest and most damning character in television comedy.
